blogs.title: The Thin Line Between Voluntary Consent and Coercion: Lessons from United States v. Coleman
blogs.description: This post dissects the Seventh Circuit’s analysis of “voluntary” consent under the Fourth Amendment, focusing on the totality‑of‑the‑circumstances test and the role of police phrasing (“I’m sensing we almost need to come inside”). It evaluates how the court weighed Lisa’s initial refusal, the officer’s repeated requests, and the absence of explicit warnings about the right to decline, and considers how this decision fits within the circuit’s evolving consent jurisprudence.

blogs.title: Scope of Third‑Party Consent in the Home: Did the Officers Overstep in United States v. Coleman?
blogs.description: An examination of the objective‑reasonableness standard for assessing the scope of consent, using the Coleman case as a lens. The article explores whether the officers’ “protective sweep” and subsequent warrant‑securement were within the bounds of Lisa’s consent, comparing the ruling to precedents such as Jimeno, Saucedo, and recent Seventh Circuit decisions on home sweeps.

blogs.title: Beyond Consent: Why Exigent Circumstances and Inevitable Discovery Were Unnecessary (and Unexplored) in United States v. Coleman
blogs.description: A critical look at the court’s decision to sideline the doctrines of exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery. The post argues that the court missed an opportunity to clarify the interplay between consent and these traditional exceptions, and probes how future cases might be affected when courts treat consent as a “catch‑all” justification.

blogs.title: Domestic Violence Calls and Fourth Amendment Rights: Policy Implications of United States v. Coleman
blogs.description: This piece places the Coleman ruling within the broader context of police responses to domestic‑violence emergencies. It assesses whether the decision encourages more proactive entry based on verbal consent, the potential impact on victims’ willingness to cooperate, and how law enforcement training might need to adjust to balance child‑safety concerns with constitutional protections.
